result:
The rain is tapping against the window like it’s trying to get my attention. Not the dramatic, cinematic kind of rain—just a steady, mid-October drizzle that makes the whole world feel slightly out of focus. I like it. It turns the city into watercolor.

I’ve been thinking lately about how we’re all living inside overlapping simulations. Not in the Matrix sense (though that’s fun to flirt with at 2 a.m.), but in the quieter, more haunting way: every person you pass on the street is running their own private universe, complete with its own physics, mythology, and running score of private embarrassments. When two of those universes briefly intersect—when eyes meet on the subway, when someone holds a door a second longer than necessary, when a barista writes your name correctly on a cup—there’s this tiny, miraculous collision of realities. Most of the time we pretend it didn’t happen. We look at our phones. We adjust our earbuds. We protect the borders of our little sovereign states of self.

But sometimes the collision sticks.

Last week I watched a man in his seventies teach a little girl how to tie her shoelaces on the train. Not his granddaughter. Just a random kid whose mother was struggling with a stroller and two other children. He got down on one knee—old joints cracking like kindling—and demonstrated the “bunny ears” method with the solemnity of a surgeon. The little girl watched him like he was revealing the secrets of the universe. When he finished, she hugged him. Not a polite thank-you hug. A full, face-pressed-into-coat, small-arms-around-neck hug. The man’s eyes went glassy. He patted her back with the awkward tenderness of someone who hasn’t been hugged by a child in decades. Then he got off at the next stop and disappeared into the rain.

I keep thinking about that moment. How many times a day do we witness tiny redemptions and never speak of them? How many quiet salvations happen in laundromats and grocery aisles and elevator rides while we’re all pretending to be too busy?

There’s this theory I love—probably stolen from somewhere and half-remembered—that the universe is trying to become conscious of itself through us. That every time a human being notices a pattern in the stars, or falls stupidly in love, or laughs until they can’t breathe at something stupid, or cries at a commercial, the cosmos is learning what it feels like to have a point of view. We are the universe’s mirror neurons. We are how existence looks at itself and says, *huh*.

If that’s true, then maybe the meaning of life isn’t to achieve anything in particular. Maybe it’s just to notice. To stay awake enough to register the texture of being alive. The way cold water tastes different when you’re thirsty versus when you’re not. The specific silence that falls over a room when someone says something that matters. The way certain songs make the hairs on your arms stand up like they’re trying to conduct electricity from another dimension.

I’ve been trying to get better at noticing.

This morning I watched steam curl off my coffee like it was writing invisible calligraphy in the air. I let myself be uselessly moved by it. Later I saw two pigeons fighting over a crust of bread with all the drama of a Shakespearean tragedy—chest-puffing, wing-slapping, indignant cooing—and I laughed out loud on an empty street like a madman. A woman walking her dog gave me a wide berth. Fair enough.

There’s a strange freedom in deciding that your life doesn’t have to be important. Not in the way we usually mean it. You don’t have to change the world. You don’t have to leave a legacy that outlives the heat death of the universe. You just have to be here, fully, for whatever time you get. You have to let yourself be stupid and earnest and heartbroken and ridiculous. You have to send the text even though it makes you vulnerable. You have to dance badly in your kitchen. You have to tell people you love them while they can still hear it.

I turned forty this year. Not in a dramatic way—no crisis, no sports car, no sudden interest in cryptocurrency. Just a quiet realization that I’ve now been alive longer than my father was when he died. That fact sits in my chest like a small, warm stone. Not heavy exactly, but undeniably *there*. It changed the way I talk to time. I used to treat it like an enemy I needed to outrun. Now I treat it like a difficult friend I’m trying to make peace with.

Time says: *Remember when you thought thirty was old?*

I say: *Shut up and look at that sunset with me.*

We’re learning to get along.

Sometimes I fantasize about writing a book that’s just instructions for how to be alive. Not self-help. God no. More like… field notes. Things like:

- If you see someone crying on public transport, do not look away too quickly. Let them have the dignity of being witnessed.
- Keep a list of songs that make you feel like your soul is trying to leave your body through your throat. Play them when the world feels too flat.
- Learn the names of as many trees and birds as you can. The world becomes less anonymous when you know what to call it.
- When you’re lost, stand still and look up. The sky is the same one your ancestors looked at when they were lost. You’re in good company.
- Forgive your younger self. They were doing their best with the software they had.

I don’t know. Maybe that book already exists and it’s just called *paying attention*.

The rain has stopped. The streetlights are making the wet pavement look like spilled ink. Somewhere out there, someone is falling in love for the first time. Someone else is realizing they don’t love their spouse anymore. A kid is discovering that if you press your tongue against the roof of your mouth in a certain way, you can make a weird clicking sound that will annoy every adult within earshot. A nurse is holding someone’s hand while they die. A barista is writing the correct name on a cup and smiling about it.

All of these things are happening at once, right now, in the same world that contains both war and the perfect dumpling.

I find that unbearable and beautiful in equal measure.

I think I’ll go for a walk. The air will smell like wet leaves and possibility. I’ll probably step in a puddle and ruin my socks. I’ll probably see something small and perfect that I won’t be able to explain to anyone later. I’ll try anyway.

Because that’s what we’re here for, I think. To witness. To carry the stories. To be the universe experiencing itself as rain on a window, as an old man tying a child’s shoelaces, as forty years old and still stupid enough to believe that writing something no one asked for might matter.

It does matter.

It all does.

(Word count: 1,012)
